query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, alumina‐forming surface coating applied to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will prevent oxygen ingress at high temperature, thereby overcoming its poor oxidation resistance without degrading its inherent mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin alumina-forming coating (via processes such as CVD, PVD, or pack cementation) to the surface of the alloy.
generation.conditions: Exposure at about 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere (air) for an extended duration (e.g., 100 hours) while under typical tensile loading strain rates encountered in prior tests.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 barrier layer on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: The coating reacts (or is pre-deposited) to form a stable Al2O3 film that effectively isolates the substrate from oxygen, thereby minimizing oxidation-driven degradation without altering the bulk microstructure that grants useful mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in oxidation (evidenced by lower weight gain and absence of internal oxide penetration) while retaining room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength values comparable to the uncoated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, which shows poor oxygen resistance at high temperatures leading to degradation of its mechanical performance over time.
generation.boundary: Results are expected under high-temperature, oxidizing conditions (around 1000 °C, in air, for up to 100 hours) and under quasi-static tensile strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1; durability under thermal cycling or fatigue is not addressed by this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how well the coating adheres during prolonged thermal exposure and whether thermal stresses or cyclic loading could cause spallation, which might compromise both oxidation resistance and mechanical performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples from identical as-cast material; apply the alumina-forming coating only to one set. Expose both sets to 1000 °C in air for 100 hours. After exposure, perform weight-gain measurements, microstructural examinations (e.g., cross-sectional SEM/EDS), and mechanical tests (tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1).
measurements: Weight change per unit area to assess oxidation kinetics
Microstructural integrity and oxide layer continuity via microscopy
Tensile yield strength and ductility comparison between coated and uncoated samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples exhibit oxidation levels (weight gain and oxide penetration) and/or mechanical property degradation (significantly reduced tensile ductility or yield strength) comparable to or worse than the uncoated samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on Mechanical Properties of Equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr Alloys

Abstract: AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

Conclusions: The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen
